title: Breadth or depth for transfer
statement: Does transfer to unpredictable test content come from covering many knowledge areas broadly or fewer ideas in depth?
detail: The reading-comprehension BrainLift bets on breadth because state-test topics are unpredictable: many knowledge networks, Tier-2 vocabulary and taught comprehension monitoring (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/teaching-reading-comprehension-brainlift.md`). The curriculum-architecture BrainLift, summarising a 2011 review of international comparisons, says high-performing jurisdictions teach fewer topics per grade in greater depth (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback2/WF - Curriculum Architecture Br - 260713-123107.md`).
against: The depth side rests on a review that the same BrainLift calls policy-facing and advocacy-oriented rather than neutral, with limited empirical evidence linking design to achievement gains (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback2/WF - Curriculum Architecture Br - 260713-123107.md`).

evidence.quote: so the only rational hedge is breadth: many knowledge networks + Tier-2 vocabulary + taught comprehension monitoring.
High-performing jurisdictions teach fewer topics per grade with greater depth. "Fewer things in greater depth" is the core design principle.
Policy-facing and advocacy-oriented rather than neutral analysis.
Limited empirical evidence directly linking design to achievement gains.
